claim: Loud sound onsets are a dominant feature coded by auditory cortex neurons projecting to primary visual cortex (V1).
source: Using two-photon calcium imaging in identified cell types in awake, head-fixed mice, we show that, among the basic features of a sound envelope, loud sound onsets are a dominant feature coded by the auditory cortex neurons projecting to primary visual cortex (V1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from two-photon calcium imaging experiments showing the distribution of sound envelope features in V1-projecting neurons.

claim: A small number of layer 1 interneurons gates cross-modal information flow from auditory cortex to V1 in a context-dependent manner.
source: In V1, a small number of layer 1 interneurons gates this cross-modal information flow in a context-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from two-photon calcium imaging of identified interneurons in layer 1 of V1.

claim: In dark conditions, auditory cortex inputs lead to suppression of the V1 population.
source: In dark conditions, auditory cortex inputs lead to suppression of the V1 population.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing V1 neuronal responses to auditory stimuli in darkness.

claim: When sound input coincides with a visual stimulus, visual responses are boosted in V1, most strongly after loud sound onsets.
source: However, when sound input coincides with a visual stimulus, visual responses are boosted in V1, most strongly after loud sound onsets.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from bimodal stimulation experiments showing enhanced visual responses when paired with sounds.

claim: A dynamic, asymmetric circuit connecting AC and V1 contributes to the encoding of visual events that are coincident with sounds.
source: Thus, a dynamic, asymmetric circuit connecting AC and V1 contributes to the encoding of visual events that are coincident with sounds.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing context-dependent modulation and boosting effects.

claim: Audition and vision have strong perceptual bonds as demonstrated by multisensory illusions.
source: Numerous multisensory illusions (Bonath et al., 2007; Maeda et al., 2004; Sekuler et al., 1997; Shams et al., 2000) show that audition and vision have strong perceptual bonds.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on multisensory illusions.

claim: In the double flash illusion, a brief sequence of two sounds played during a single visual flash leads to the perception of two flashes.
source: For example, in the double flash illusion (Shams et al., 2000) a brief sequence of two sounds played during a single visual flash leads to the perception of two flashes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research on the double flash illusion.

claim: The superior colliculus is one of the best studied integrative regions where visual and auditory cues are combined in networks computing gaze direction.
source: One of the best studied integrative regions is the superior colliculus, where visual and auditory cues are combined in the networks computing gaze direction (Stein and Stanford, 2008; Witten and Knudsen, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on the superior colliculus.

claim: Functional auditory-visual interactions exist in primary sensory cortex.
source: increasing evidence shows that functional auditory-visual interactions exist already in primary sensory cortex (Ibrahim et al., 2016; Iurilli et al., 2012; Kayser et al., 2010; Kayser et al., 2008; Meijer et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research demonstrating auditory-visual interactions in primary sensory cortex.

claim: Numerous direct connections exist between primary auditory and visual cortex.
source: Moreover, axonal tracing studies indicate that numerous direct connections exist between primary auditory and visual cortex (Bizley et al., 2007; Driver and Noesselt, 2008; Falchier et al., 2002; Ghazanfar and Schroeder, 2006; Innocenti et al., 1988; Leinweber et al., 2017; Zingg et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to axonal tracing studies.

claim: Auditory to visual connections are much stronger than their reciprocals.
source: Recent studies indicate that auditory to visual connections are much stronger than their reciprocals, and that they provide inputs to visual cortex that can modulate visually driven activity (Ibrahim et al., 2016; Iurilli et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent studies on auditory-visual connections.

claim: Mouse auditory cortex encodes a wide variety of acoustic features.
source: Mouse auditory cortex encodes a wide variety of acoustic features (Mizrahi et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research on mouse auditory cortex.

claim: Spectral content and temporal features such as modulations of frequency or intensity are the most well-studied features in auditory cortex.
source: Spectral content (Issa et al., 2014; Kanold et al., 2014) and temporal features such as modulations of frequency (Trujillo et al., 2011) or intensity (Gao and Wehr, 2015) are the most well-studied
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on auditory cortex feature encoding.

claim: Intensity variations occurring at sound onsets and offsets are particularly salient auditory features.
source: intensity variations occurring at sound onsets and offsets (Deneux et al., 2016b; Scholl et al., 2010) are particularly salient auditory features.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on sound onset and offset encoding.

claim: Temporal coincidence is used for perceptually assigning auditory and visual stimuli to the same object.
source: In contrast, temporal coincidence is known to be used for perceptually assigning auditory and visual stimuli to the same object and is implicated in the double flash (Slutsky and Recanzone, 2001) and ventriloquist illusions (Bonath et al., 2007; Recanzone, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on temporal coincidence in multisensory perception.

claim: Covariations of the size of a visual input and sound intensity envelope are important for binding looming and receding auditory-visual stimuli.
source: Also, covariations of the size of a visual input and sound intensity envelope are important for binding looming and receding auditory-visual stimuli (Tyll et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research on audiovisual binding.

claim: Some neurons in auditory cortex respond only to high amplitude, 'loud' sound onsets, whereas others only respond to low amplitude, 'quiet' onsets.
source: Some neurons respond only to high amplitude, 'loud' sound onsets, whereas others only respond to low amplitude, 'quiet' onsets, and neurons responding to offsets and sustained phases are also tuned to precise intensity ranges (Deneux et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research on intensity tuning in auditory cortex neurons.

claim: Mechanical shocks produce sounds that rise abruptly in intensity and tend to activate loud onset neurons.
source: For example, mechanical shocks produce sounds that rise abruptly in intensity and tend to activate loud onset neurons, while more continuous events produce sounds that progressively ramp up in intensity and first activate quiet onset neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about how different types of sounds activate different neuron types.

claim: V1-projecting neurons in auditory cortex are predominantly tuned to loud onsets.
source: we used two-photon calcium imaging and intersectional genetics to identify some of the intensity envelope features encoded by AC neurons that project to V1, and showed that V1-projecting neurons are predominantly tuned to loud onsets while other tested envelope features are less prominently represented
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from two-photon calcium imaging of retrogradely labeled V1-projecting neurons.

claim: Cross-modal information from auditory cortex impacts V1 in a context-dependent manner, with a net inhibitory effect in darkness and a net positive effect in the light.
source: We also show that this cross-modal information impacts V1 in a context-dependent manner, with a net inhibitory effect in darkness and a net positive effect in the light, probably mediated by a subpopulation of L1 inhibitory neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing different V1 responses to auditory stimuli in dark versus light conditions.

claim: The context-dependent mechanism allows for a boosting of visual responses that occurs together with auditory events, particularly when those include loud sound onsets.
source: Furthermore, we show that this mechanism also allows for a boosting of visual responses that occurs together with auditory events, particularly when those include loud sound onsets, increasing the saliency of visual events that co-occur with abrupt sounds.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from bimodal stimulation experiments.

claim: V1-projecting neurons in auditory cortex are located predominantly in layer 5.
source: Consistent with previous reports, we observed that these neurons were located predominantly in layer 5 (Figure 1B) (Ibrahim et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observation and citation to previous research.

claim: Loud onset responses represented 48% of the clustered neurons in V1-projecting cells, and only 36% and 21% in layer 5 and layer 2/3, respectively.
source: the largest discrepancies were observed for neurons signaling loud onsets which represented 48% of the clustered neurons in V1-projecting cells, and only 36% and 21% in layer 5 and layer 2/3, respectively (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of clustered neuronal responses shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Loud onset responses were enriched in layer 5 which contains most of the cells with direct projections to V1 and predominant in cells retrogradely labeled as V1-projecting neurons.
source: Thus, loud onset responses were enriched in layer 5 which contains most of the cells with direct projections to V1 and predominant in cells retrogradely labeled as V1-projecting neurons
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing distribution of response types across layers and cell types.

claim: Other envelope features are also conveyed by V1-projecting cells.
source: indicating that AC is organized to favor the transfer of this particular sound envelope information even if other envelope features are also conveyed by V1-projecting cells (Figure 1C)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating multiple response types in V1-projecting neurons.

claim: V1-projecting cells convey some sound frequency information.
source: as well as some sound frequency information (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Sounds occasionally triggered predominantly horizontal saccadic eye movements, especially sounds with loud onsets.
source: We found that sounds occasionally triggered predominantly horizontal saccadic eye movements, especially sounds with loud onsets (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by eye tracking data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Sound-induced changes in pupil diameter were observed.
source: Sound-induced changes in pupil diameter were also observed (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by pupil tracking data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Saccades triggered responses in V1 in the lit condition.
source: In the lit condition, the saccades triggered responses in V1 (e.g. Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Sounds alone trigger responses in supra-granular V1 neurons.
source: After this correction, we pooled together the activity of 18925 V1 neurons (35 sessions, nine mice) and observed that sounds alone trigger responses in supra-granular V1 neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from two-photon calcium imaging of V1 neurons.

claim: The responses to sounds in V1 were stronger for the down-ramping sounds, similar to what was seen in the activity of V1-projecting AC neurons.
source: The responses were stronger for the down-ramping sounds, similar to what we saw in the activity of V1-projecting AC neurons (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of data from V1 and V1-projecting AC neurons shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: The net population response in V1 was globally excitatory when mice were in the light and inhibitory when mice were in complete darkness.
source: Strikingly however, we observed that the net population response was globally excitatory when mice were in the light and inhibitory when mice were in complete darkness (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing V1 responses in light versus dark conditions shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: The observed inhibition in V1 in darkness was seen consistently across cells and sound presentations, likely corresponding to a transient decrease in basal firing rates.
source: The observed inhibition was seen consistently across cells and sound presentations, likely corresponding to a transient decrease in basal firing rates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and inference about the mechanism.

claim: Covering the contralateral eye was sufficient to obtain the same inhibition as in darkness.
source: Interestingly, covering the contralateral eye was sufficient to obtain the same inhibition as in darkness (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), suggesting a possible role of direct unilateral visual inputs in the context dependence of auditory responses in V1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Excitatory responses to sounds in the light cannot be attributed to sound-induced pupil dilation as these movements occurred after V1 responses.
source: Also, excitatory responses to sounds in the light cannot be attributed to sound-induced pupil dilation as these movements occurred after V1 responses (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is based on temporal analysis of pupil dilation and V1 responses shown in Figure 3B.

claim: V1 implements a mechanism that inverts the impact of AC inputs depending on whether or not visual information is available.
source: Taking these results together, we conclude that V1 implements a mechanism that inverts the impact of AC inputs depending on whether or not visual information is available.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing context-dependent responses.

claim: Areas next to V1 (secondary visual or associative areas) displayed excitatory responses in both the lit and dark conditions, unlike V1.
source: Unlike V1, these areas displayed excitatory responses in both the lit and dark conditions (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing V1 and neighboring areas shown in Figure 3D.

claim: No response modulation between the dark and lit conditions was observed in V1-projecting neurons of auditory cortex.
source: We observed no response modulation between the dark and lit conditions (Figure 3F), indicating that context-dependent modulation arises in V1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from imaging V1-projecting AC neurons shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Context-dependent auditory inputs to V1 are mediated by direct AC to V1 projections.
source: Finally, we verified that, as suggested by previous studies (Ibrahim et al., 2016; Iurilli et al., 2012), context-dependent auditory inputs to V1 are mediated by direct AC to V1 projections.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from AC inactivation experiments and citations to previous studies.

claim: Injections of muscimol into AC almost completely abolished auditory responses in V1 and in the neighboring areas.
source: Injections of the GABA-receptor agonist muscimol into AC during imaging almost completely abolished auditory responses in V1 and in the neighboring areas (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from muscimol inactivation experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Targeted chemogenetic inhibition of V1-projecting neurons in AC produced a decrease of sound responses in V1.
source: We also used targeted chemogenetic inhibition (systemic CNO injections) of V1-projecting neurons in AC, expressing the hM4Di channel by co-injection of a CAV-Cre virus in V1 and an AAV8-flex-hM4di in AC (Figure 4). This produced a decrease of sound responses which was consistent across sound repetitions for the imaged neural population (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from chemogenetic inhibition experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: In layer 2/3, both excitatory and inhibitory neurons were globally inhibited by sounds in the dark and excited in the light.
source: We observed that in layer 2/3 both excitatory (n = 4348) and inhibitory neurons (n = 726) were globally inhibited by sounds in the dark and excited in the light
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from imaging identified excitatory and inhibitory neurons in layer 2/3.

claim: The layer 1 interneuron population seemed globally unaffected in the dark and excited in the light.
source: while the layer 1 interneuron population seemed globally unaffected in the dark and excited in the light (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from imaging layer 1 interneurons shown in Figure 5B.

claim: A subpopulation of 12.8% of all L1 inhibitory neurons were significantly activated in the dark.
source: we found a large fraction of neurons significantly inhibited, but also, a subpopulation of 12.8% of all L1 inhibitory neurons that were significantly activated in the dark (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of single neuron responses shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Only 2.1% of inhibitory and 1% of excitatory cells in L2/3 were significantly activated by sounds in the dark.
source: This positive response was rare in L2/3 with only 2.1% of inhibitory and 1% of excitatory cells significantly activated (chance levels = 1%, Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of single neuron responses shown in Figure 5C.

claim: L1 neurons that are excited by sounds in the dark tend to be less excited in the light.
source: it is apparent that the L1 neurons that are excited by sounds in the dark tend to be less excited in the light (e.g. Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of individual neuron responses shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: L1 neurons inhibited or unaffected by sounds in the dark became more activated in the light.
source: In contrast, L1 neurons inhibited or unaffected by sounds in the dark became more activated in the light (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of individual neuron responses shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A significant percentage (5.3%) of L1 neurons respond less in light than in dark.
source: Consistently, statistical assessment showed that a significant percentage (5.3%) of L1 neurons (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.01) respond less in light than in dark (Figure 5F)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Almost all L1 neurons that respond less in light than in dark are significantly excited in the dark (4.9%).
source: and that almost all these neurons are significantly excited in the dark (4.9%, Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: There was no significant population of L2/3 neurons that responded less in the light than in the dark.
source: In contrast, based on the same tests, there was no significant population of L2/3 neurons that responded less in the light than in the dark (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5F,G.

claim: Layer 1 contains the only supragranular subpopulation of GABAergic neurons that can provide a context-dependent, sound-induced inhibition gated by visual inputs.
source: Thus, we conclude that layer 1 contains the only supragranular subpopulation of GABAergic neurons that can provide a context-dependent, sound-induced inhibition gated by visual inputs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data comparing L1 and L2/3 interneurons.

claim: 11% of the V1 neurons displayed significant supra-additive boosting of their visual responses when coincident with the loud onset of down-ramps.
source: We first observed that 11% of the V1 neurons displayed significant (Generalized Linear Model, p<0.05) supra-additive boosting of their visual responses when coincident with the loud onset of down-ramps (e.g. Figure 6A)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of bimodal responses shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The boosting effect is visible at the population level and dependent on AC as assessed with muscimol silencing.
source: an effect even visible at the population level (Figure 6B) and dependent on AC as assessed with muscimol silencing (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by population data and AC inactivation experiments shown in Figure 6B,D,E.

claim: Clustering of bimodal responses identified seven distinct clusters capturing 49.5 ± 11.2% of the response variance.
source: This analysis identified seven distinct clusters (Figure 6C) capturing 49.5 ± 11.2% of the response variance.
evidence: The claim is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Four clusters responded more to looming than receding disks, and three clusters had the opposite preference.
source: Four clusters (#1,4,6,7; 358 neurons) responded more to looming than receding disks, and three clusters (#2,3,5; 141 neurons) had the opposite preference.
evidence: The claim is supported by clustering analysis of visual responses.

claim: Down-ramping sounds boosted the responses of all cell clusters that responded to the onset of visual stimuli.
source: Down-ramping sounds boosted the responses of all cell clusters that responded to the onset of visual stimuli. (Figure 6C, black arrows for clusters 1–5, bootstrap test, see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of bimodal responses shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Very little boosting was observed with the quiet onset of up-ramps, consistent with its reduced representation in AC to V1 projections.
source: Very little boosting was observed with the quiet onset of up-ramps (Figure 6C), consistent with its reduced representation in AC to V1 projections (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of bimodal responses to different sound types and relates to earlier findings.

claim: Visual responses in V1 are boosted preferentially by the coincidence of loud sound onsets with respect to other basic envelope features.
source: Our data suggest that visual responses in V1 are boosted preferentially by the coincidence of loud sound onsets with respect to other basic envelope features.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data on bimodal responses.

claim: A moderate response suppression was observed, but only in cluster 7.
source: Note that a moderate response suppression was also observed, but only in cluster 7 (Figure 6C, blue arrow).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The boosting of visual responses appeared to be a strong feature of V1, as the same analysis identified only one supra-linear cluster out of six clusters in the associative area medial to V1.
source: Moreover, the boosting of visual responses appeared to be a strong feature of V1, as the same analysis identified only one supra-linear cluster out of six clusters in the associative area medial to V1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of V1 and neighboring area responses shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A minimal model in which AC projections excite both a population of excitatory neurons and a population of interneurons in V1 can explain context-dependent sound-driven inhibition and boosting of visual responses.
source: To propose a mechanism, we established a minimal model in which AC projections excite both a population of excitatory neurons (pyramidal cells) and a population of interneurons in V1 (putatively, the identified L1 population), consistent with connectivity studies (Ibrahim et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on computational modeling informed by experimental data and previous connectivity studies.

claim: The subpopulation of L1 interneurons that are less responsive to sounds in light also have a smaller baseline fluorescence in light.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the subpopulation of L1 interneurons that are less responsive to sounds in light also have a smaller baseline fluorescence in light, an effect that is not observed for other L1 interneurons (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of baseline fluorescence shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The model can reproduce boosting of visual responses by sounds if excitatory neurons have a simple non-linear response function with a low, subthreshold output gain and a high, supra-threshold gain.
source: We then showed that the same model can reproduce boosting of visual responses by sounds (Figure 7D,E) if excitatory neurons also have a simple non-linear response function. When excitatory neurons have a low, subthreshold output gain and a high, supra-threshold gain (Figure 7A), it is possible to reproduce the observations that the response to sound alone (low gain regime) is weaker than the bimodal boosting effect (high-gain regime) (Figure 7D–E).
evidence: The claim is based on computational modeling shown in Figure 7.

claim: Sound-driven boosting of visual responses could rely on dendritic calcium spikes in apical dendrites of layer 2/3 pyramidal cells.
source: Apical dendrites of layer 2/3 pyramidal cells are known to produce large calcium spikes which boost somatic output when somatic activity coincides with excitatory inputs arriving in the apical tree (Larkum et al., 2007). As AC axon terminals are concentrated in layer 1 where they likely contact the apical dendrites of pyramidal cells, sound-driven boosting of visual responses could rely on this dendritic phenomenon.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from known dendritic properties and anatomical connectivity, supported by citation.

claim: A minimal circuit including a direct excitation from auditory cortex onto L2/3 pyramidal cells and an indirect inhibition via a subpopulation of L1 interneurons is sufficient to provide a context-dependent auditory modulation that emphasizes visual events coincident with loud sound onsets.
source: Taken together, our data and modeling indicate that a minimal circuit including a direct excitation from auditory cortex onto L2/3 pyramidal cells and an indirect inhibition via a subpopulation of L1 interneurons is sufficient to provide a context-dependent auditory modulation that emphasizes visual events coincident with loud sound onsets.
evidence: The claim is based on integration of experimental data and computational modeling.

claim: V1-projecting neurons have a different bias in the distribution of sound envelope features they encode, as compared to layer 2/3 neurons in AC and also to layer 5 in which they are located.
source: First, we showed that V1-projecting neurons have a different bias in the distribution of sound envelope features they encode, as compared to layer 2/3 neurons in AC and also, although to a lesser extent, as compared to layer 5 in which they are located.
evidence: The claim summarizes findings from the experimental data on feature distributions.

claim: The V1-projecting neuron population predominantly encodes loud sound onsets.
source: In particular, the V1-projecting neuron population predominantly encodes loud sound onsets.
evidence: The claim summarizes a key finding from the experimental data.

claim: V1-projecting neurons are gated by a context-dependent inhibitory mechanism likely implemented by a subpopulation of L1 interneurons.
source: Second, they are gated by a context-dependent inhibitory mechanism likely implemented by a subpopulation of L1 interneurons.
evidence: The claim summarizes findings from the experimental data on context-dependent responses.

claim: The impact of AC inputs on V1 representations is to produce a strong boosting of responses to dynamical visual stimuli coincident with different sound envelope features, particularly with loud sound onsets.
source: Third, their impact on V1 representations is to produce a strong boosting of responses to dynamical visual stimuli coincident with different sound envelope features, particularly with loud sound onsets.
evidence: The claim summarizes findings from the bimodal stimulation experiments.

claim: In layer 2/3, there is a balance between the main neuron types that signal the beginning and the end of sounds with equivalent fractions of neurons responding to quiet or loud onsets and loud offsets.
source: As observed earlier, in layer 2/3, there is a balance between the main neuron types that signal the beginning and the end of sounds with equivalent fractions of neurons responding to quiet or loud onsets and loud offsets (Figure 1F, note that 'tonic +loud OFF' neurons are included in this count. Quiet offset neurons are rare and not robustly detected across datasets. Detection of tonic responses by clustering is also variable.).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F and relates to previous observations.

claim: In upper layer 5, the distribution becomes more biased toward loud onsets at the expense of offset neurons.
source: In upper layer 5, the distribution becomes more biased toward loud onsets at the expense of offset neurons
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of feature distributions across layers.

claim: In the layer 5-located V1-projecting cells, half of the neurons respond to loud onsets and 10% of the cells to loud offsets.
source: a trend that is further increased in the layer 5-located V1-projecting cells in which half of the neurons respond to loud onsets and 10% of the cells to loud offsets.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of V1-projecting neuron responses.

claim: Similar results have been found in somatosensory cortex for neurons projecting to secondary somatosensory or motor cortex.
source: Similar results have been found in somatosensory cortex for neurons projecting to secondary somatosensory or motor cortex (Chen et al., 2013a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research in somatosensory cortex.

claim: Projection specificity can be a determinant of feature selectivity, at least for some intensity modulation features at sound onsets and offsets.
source: Our results show that projection specificity can also be a determinant of feature selectivity, at least for some intensity modulation features at sound onsets and offsets.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental findings on feature distributions in projection neurons.

claim: Layer 2/3 neurons in V1 are more impacted by abrupt sounds with loud onsets than by sounds with softer onsets.
source: As a result of these fine adjustments of feature distributions, layer 2/3 neurons in V1 are more impacted by abrupt sounds with loud onsets (e.g. down-ramps) than by sounds with softer onsets (e.g. up-ramps).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data on V1 responses to different sound types.

claim: The asymmetry in V1 responses to different sound types is particularly striking for excitatory effects seen in light or with visual stimuli, but less pronounced for inhibitory effects in the dark.
source: This asymmetry is particularly striking for excitatory effects seen in light or with visual stimuli (Figures 3B and 6), but less pronounced for inhibitory effects in the dark (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of data from different experimental conditions.

claim: L2/3 V1 pyramidal cells may receive projections almost exclusively from AC loud onset neurons while interneurons providing inhibition in the dark still receive a significant fraction of quiet onset and loud offset inputs.
source: It is thus possible that the projection targets also depend on encoded features. For example, L2/3 V1 pyramidal cells may receive projections almost exclusively from AC loud onset neurons while interneurons providing inhibition in the dark still receive a significant fraction of quiet onset and loud offset inputs.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed asymmetries in responses.

claim: Context-dependent inhibition could serve to decrease V1 activity in the dark when visual information is irrelevant for sound source localization, while leaving possibilities to integrate auditory and visual information in light conditions.
source: First, it reconciles conflicting reports of sound-induced inhibition or excitation in V1 (Ibrahim et al., 2016; Iurilli et al., 2012). Second, context-dependent inhibition could serve to decrease V1 activity in the dark when visual information is irrelevant for sound source localization, while leaving possibilities to integrate auditory and visual information in light conditions.
evidence: The claim is speculative about the functional role of context-dependent inhibition.

claim: The context-dependence of auditory responses in V1 is reminiscent of the observation that AC to V1 projections, activated by loud sounds and acting through L1, boost preferred orientation responses in V1 and inhibit non-preferred orientations.
source: The context-dependence of auditory responses in V1 is reminiscent of the recent observation that AC to V1 projections, activated by loud sounds and acting through L1, boost preferred orientation responses in V1 and inhibit non-preferred orientations (Ibrahim et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim relates current findings to previous research through citation.

claim: Only VIP-negative interneurons receive AC inputs in V1.
source: compatible with the observation that only VIP-negative interneurons receive AC inputs in V1 (Ibrahim et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: L1 interneurons serve other functions such as disinhibition of L2/3 in various contexts.
source: and the observation that L1 interneurons serve other functions (Hattori et al., 2017), such as disinhibition of L2/3 in various contexts (Fu et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2013; Letzkus et al., 2015; Pfeffer et al., 2013; Pi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on L1 interneuron functions.

claim: Visual responses in AC do not modulate a fraction of the AC input to V1, based on context-independent responses of retrogradely identified V1-projecting cells.
source: We can however exclude that visual responses in AC (Morrill and Hasenstaub, 2018) modulate a fraction of the AC input to V1, based on context-independent responses of retrogradely identified V1-projecting cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data and citation to previous research.

claim: The context-dependence of auditory responses is restricted to V1 and not observed in associative areas.
source: Interestingly, our data obtained outside V1 indicate that, independent of the exact mechanism of context-dependence of auditory responses, this phenomenon is restricted to V1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of V1 and neighboring area responses.

claim: AC projections to associative areas impact the local circuit differently than in V1.
source: This indicates that AC projections to associative areas impact the local circuit differently than in V1.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed differences between V1 and associative areas.

claim: The large amplitude of the sound-induced boosting as compared to the weaker responses observed when sounds are played without coincident visual input points toward a threshold mechanism.
source: The large amplitude of the sound-induced boosting as compared to the weaker responses observed when sounds are played without coincident visual input (Figures 3 and 5 vs Figure 6, see also Figure 7) points toward a threshold mechanism, allowing for amplification of the auditory input only if sufficient visual input concomitantly arrives.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparison of unimodal and bimodal responses.

claim: Amplification of L1 input by coincident somatic inputs triggering calcium spikes in apical dendrites has been described both in L5 and L2/3 pyramidal cells.
source: For example, amplification of L1 input by coincident somatic inputs triggering calcium spikes in apical dendrites has been described both in L5 (Larkum et al., 1999) and L2/3 (Larkum et al., 2007) pyramidal cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on dendritic mechanisms.
